::: {.callout-tip title="Newest: the planner runs the indirect lift from rest"}
Given only the indirect lift's formation sequence, the search realizes the
lift quasi-statically in MuJoCo at disk friction 0.4 and 0.5, and not at
0.3. See [The planner runs the indirect lift from rest](indirect-lift.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="The runs below this box predate the current configuration"}
Every run on this page outside [the indirect lift](indirect-lift.qmd) was
measured with the simulator's disk–box friction at **0.99** and the gate and
tracker at **0.35** (the gate at the simulator's 0.99 before the evening of
Nov 9), before the
declared band μ<sub>disk</sub> ∈ [0.3, 0.5] with the gate and tracker at 0.3;
with **release edits on** except in the quasi-static lift (releases are now off: their rules were dropped as
hand rules, and a principled release is a proposal); with Λ<sub>qs</sub> before
its current default options; and without the workspace and dynamic-event rules
of the paper's search, and at the friction above, unless a section says so.
Most lifts below let the box drop onto the platform; the current target is the indirect lift, held at every
instant. The rerun at the band's ends with every rule on is pending. These
results are the record of those configurations, not the current planner's.
:::

Below the newest result come [the night of November 9–10](#nov10), when the
search did the whole task end to end, then [November 9](#nov9), on elliptic friction
contacts. [The last section](#pyramidal) summarizes the November 8–9 runs on
MuJoCo's pyramidal contacts, before the redesign.

Each clip replays calls that the planner actually made in its teacher runs
(branch `phase1/planar`). No motion here was staged for the
video. The search chose the edits (the contact changes), and each edit was
executed by the local solver the run used: the quasi-static realizer Λ_qs or
a learned skill Λ_RL (see [The local solver](../planar-build/local-solver.qmd)).
Each call was re-run in MJX from the logged start state, recorded, and
drawn. The re-run was checked against the log: the same success, the same
end formation, and the end pose within a few millimetres. One clip that did
not match is labelled **DIVERGED** below.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## How to read a clip

- **View.** From the side, with +x to the **left**, as in the paper. The
  green surface is the platform, the grey one the floor, the blue ball the
  disk. A red stripe marks the face the box rests on at the start, so you
  can follow its rotation.
- **Top-left box.** The task and instance; the current segment *k/n* with its
  edit and formations (σ → σ′); the solver that ran it; the formation the
  recognizer reads right now, with **[TIE]** when two formations can't be
  told apart; and whether the re-run matched the log.
- **Speed.** Stated in the overlay at every moment. Λ_qs calls are about
  21 s long and mostly at rest, so they play at 3× while the box rests and
  in real time while it moves. The learned skills act in a fraction of a
  second, so their first 0.6 s plays at 0.25× (slow motion).
- **Cards.** A short hold after each segment, then the strict test's verdict
  (SOLVED, or FAILED with the clause that failed).
:::

## Night of November 9–10: end to end {#nov10}

::: {.callout-warning title="These runs used a temporary ±20 cm push range"}
The end-to-end, lower-friction and quasi-static runs in this section ran
with the transport's push range widened from the stock ±5 cm to **±20 cm**, a
temporary setting; it is not a direction, and the parametric certificate
(below) is to replace it. A
single push could then move the box up to 200 mm. This was not stated here
before (it was set outside the recorded run options). The teacher runs, the
learned-ranker comparison and the November 9 results below use the stock
range. Without the wider range the end-to-end task fails: see [the push range
decides the task](#push-range).
:::

Overnight the search did the whole task: **lift the box onto the platform and
push it to a set place there**. The task (`lift_to`) asks for the box's centre
at x = 0.25 ± 0.01 m on the platform, at rest. On 16 instances the redesign
solves **13** (Wilson 95%: 57–93%), and **15** with the last push aimed at the
window's centre (described below; the default since November 10), both with
the ±20 cm push range. Every solve takes the same route:

push to the riser → make s → **pivot** → **release** onto {t} → disk to the
box's side face → **push** → **push** to the window.

<video src="media/d23/liftto_00000_solved.mp4" controls muted playsinline preload="metadata" width="100%"></video>

**lift_to, instance 0: SOLVED in 180 calls**, 7 on the path, every call a
success; the box ends at x = 0.243 m. The replay reproduces all 7 calls to
0.0 mm.

<video src="media/d23/liftto_00002_solved.mp4" controls muted playsinline preload="metadata" width="100%"></video>

**lift_to, instance 2: SOLVED in 196 calls.** One call on the path (a release
the realizer did not finish) still pushed the box 108 mm along the platform;
the search kept that outcome and finished with a push to x = 0.240 m.

### What made the platform pushes work

All evening, every push along the platform was refused before the disk
moved: "the target is not in the disk's run along the contacted feature". The
cause was the disk's placement, not the mechanics. The relaxed gate put the
disk **0.8 mm past the end** of the stretch of face the controller recognises.
The fix (decided by Aykut): for a push, the disk goes to the most robust of
5 placements inside that stretch, as it already did for contact changes. In
the replays, two pushes that had moved the box 0 mm then moved it 48.6 mm and
47.2 mm.

### Where the misses stop

The solved instances end at x = 0.240–0.245 m, the **near edge** of the
window. A push toward the goal aims at the nearest of the goal poses, which
are spread across the window, so it aims at the edge, x = 0.24, and the
realizer stops a few millimetres short of its aim. Once the box is within
10 mm of a goal pose no further push counts as progress, so one instance
stalled at x = 0.2374, just outside. Aiming the last push at the window's
centre (the default since Nov 10) solves that instance (ends at x = 0.247) and
keeps the others solved. Paired on all 16 instances, the flag solves 15
against 13, loses none, and never needs more calls (median 148 against 180).
The one instance it misses fails for another reason (its long pushes came too
late in the budget).

### The push range decides the task {#push-range}

At the stock range (±5 cm per push) the same task fails: **0 of 3** instances
on November 9 and **0 of 7** on the morning of November 10 (the second run
with the push feasibility check on), 0 of 10 in all. Each 200 mm slide along
the platform becomes four or five 50 mm pushes, each needing its own approach,
and the search runs out of its 256 calls with the box about 5 cm short of the
window. The ±20 cm range works because it checks a 200 mm push as **one** call.
Doing that properly is the job of the next build, a **parametric push
certificate**: certify that the disk can push the box along the whole path,
as a function of the position along it, instead of on a fixed 5 cm grid. These
runs are the evidence for why it comes next.

### A quasi-static lift, and a caveat

With releases switched off, the search must keep the box held at every
instant (these runs also used the ±20 cm push range). On the evening's code it solved lift instance 2 that way in 52 calls,
5 on the path: the pivot, a held tilt-up from 3° to 73°, and a push over the
step's corner that leaves the box upright on the platform. The replay
reproduces all 5 calls to 0.0 mm.

<video src="media/d23/lift_00002_quasistatic.mp4" controls muted playsinline preload="metadata" width="100%"></video>

Rerun overnight with the robust disk placement, instance 1 ran out of budget
(184 calls), and instance 0 was solved through the pivot and two held
tilt-up pushes (5° → 63°), with the box finally resting on the step's corner.
But its **last** call, a transfer that the realizer did not complete, ended
with the box toppling onto the platform and being dragged about 0.8 m by the
disk, which was flung off. That end is at rest and on the platform, so the
search accepted it. It was a solve by the rules then, not a quasi-static one.
**Decided Nov 10:** such outcomes no longer count. An end with the disk outside
its workspace is invalid in every run, and quasi-static runs reject ends
reached through a dynamic event (a topple). Under these rules this instance 0
"solve" is rejected; the video stays as the example of what the rule removes.

<video src="media/d23/qs_00000_topple.mp4" controls muted playsinline preload="metadata" width="100%"></video>

### Lower friction

The same lift task with the disk–box friction lowered in both the planner and
the simulator (with the ±20 cm push range and releases on; before the friction
band, whose lower end 0.3 is now what the gate and tracker use):

40 lifting instances each, budget 192 calls, the same code throughout:

| Disk–box friction μ | Lifts solved | Wilson 95% | Median calls |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.35 (the gate's value then) | **39 of 40** | 87–100% | 109 |
| 0.2 | **36 of 40** | 77–96% | 92 |
| 0.1 | **25 of 40** | 47–76% | 100 |

Paired on the same starts (exact McNemar): 0.35 against 0.1, 15 instances
are solved only at 0.35 and 1 only at 0.1 (p ≈ 0.0005); 0.35 against 0.2,
4 against 1 (p ≈ 0.38). Lowering the friction to 0.2 costs little; at 0.1 the
lift often fails. (At μ = 0.35 this run lifts 39 of 40, where the evening's
run lifted 37; that run used the stock push range and earlier code, so the
difference is not due to the fixes alone.)

At μ = 0.1 the failures are not budget: the search runs out of moves, most
of them at the pivot, where the release onto the platform needs more friction
than there is.

### Where to put the disk on a face

The 5-placement rule is a stopgap. For a disk on a box face, the moment
couples to the disk's position s only through s·F_n, and with τ = s·F_n
(exact, since F_n ≥ 0) the set of positions where the box is held is an
interval that two linear programs find. The margin is quasi-concave in s, so
the best placement is found exactly. This rule is in the code (off by
default; the certified placement on [Certifying a whole box](../planar-build/certificate.qmd#certified-placement)
is its interval-certified version). Two findings came out of building it:

- When the box needs the disk to stand, the realizer keeps the disk where it
  already is on the box, so no placement rule, sampled or exact, is carried
  out there (errors up to 34 mm).
- The same lifting applied to **pushing** (support friction at its limit, no
  tipping, the disk sticking) gives the interval of positions from which a
  push can move the box. On 63 logged pushes it predicts failure with
  precision 0.88 and recall 0.79, and it flags pushes the holding test offers
  but that cannot move the box at all (a disk on the top face trying to drag
  it 182 mm). Since November 10 this check is on by default (Aykut's decision);
  the paired run planned for it did not run.

The literature (from sampling and scoring, as in Posa's group, to exact contact
regions for grasps, to convex relaxations) is collected in the parametric
certification review.

### The learned ranker, against a uniform ranker on the same starts

The ranker π trained yesterday evening, on **40 lifting instances from a seed
the training never saw**, at budget 64, paired with a uniform ranker on the
same 40 starts and the same code:

| Ranker | Lifts solved | Wilson 95% | Median calls |
|---|---|---|---|
| Learned π | **40 of 40** | 91–100% | 47.5 |
| Uniform | **3 of 40** | 3–20% | 52 |

The 37 instances solved only by the learned ranker against none the other way
give an exact McNemar p ≈ 1.5 × 10⁻¹¹. Two caveats: π was trained with the
older, looser lift goal (part of the box over the platform; every solve above
is graded with the full rule), and on solves that are mostly releases and
falls. With releases off, π and V₁ are to be retrained on held solves once the
search produces them.

## November 9: elliptic contacts, the redesign, and CMGMP {#nov9}

Four things happened on November 9. The simulator's friction model turned
out to be wrong for a box at rest, and was changed. The CMGMP baseline was
re-run on the new contacts. The lift's pivot was fixed. And the redesigned
search ([Search](../planar-build/search.qmd#redesign)) ran on 40 lifting and
40 lowering instances: it **lifts 37 of 40 and lowers 40 of 40**, and, paired
with CMGMP on the same starts, lifts more within 30 minutes while CMGMP is
faster at short budgets ([results below](#d23-results)).

### The simulator, not the gate, was wrong

MuJoCo's default *pyramidal* friction cones let a box creep off a rest that
the statics say is held. *Elliptic* cones (impedance ratio 10), at the same
step and contact parameters, remove the creep. On the box leaning on the step
corner with the disk pulled away:

| | pyramidal (old default) | elliptic, impratio 10 (adopted) |
|---|---|---|
| creep, °/s | 0.40 | 0.008 |
| rests held for 10 s | 0 of 84 | 84 of 84 |
| simulator agrees with the gate (poses away from the tipping boundary) | 87 of 453 | 452 of 453 |

So the gate's statics were right; the simulator let held boxes slide. Every
scene now uses elliptic cones and full float32 matrix products. The
redesigned search and CMGMP are run on them; the earlier pipeline is
superseded by the redesign and is not re-run (Aykut's decision, Nov 9). The
results further down this page, below the November 9 section, used the
pyramidal cones.

### CMGMP on elliptic contacts

CMGMP (the contact-mode-guided planner of Cheng et al., the authors' C++
code, patched for our disk's 1 N motors) ran on the 50 shared test starts,
25 per task. Each start gets up to 1,800 s; CMGMP is restarted with fresh
seeds until an executed plan passes. Every plan is executed in our MJX
simulator on elliptic contacts and graded by our strict test. A lift counts
only if the box ends *fully* on the platform, at rest.

| Task (25 starts) | within 60 s | within 300 s | within 1,800 s | plans claimed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| lift | 1 (1–20%) | 5 (9–39%) | 15 (41–77%) | 22 |
| lower | 14 (37–73%) | 21 (65–94%) | 24 (80–99%) | 25 |

95% Wilson intervals in brackets. Seeds run 0, 1, 2, …, so each budget's
column is a prefix of one run. The lift needs many restarts (median 141
planning attempts per start). An earlier grading of the same lift run used a
looser rule (the box only partly over the platform: 3 / 14 / 20) and is
superseded.

The paired comparison with our planner on these same starts is
[below](#paired).

### How CMGMP lifts

Every CMGMP lift we rendered takes the same route, read by our formation
recognizer:

```text
{g} → {m_x, g} → {m_x, s, g} → {m_x, g_v, s_v} → {m_x, s_v} → {m_x, t}
```

The disk pushes the box against the riser and tips it into **our pivot
formation** {m_x, g_v, s_v}. The floor corner lets go and the box hangs on the
step corner, {m_x, s_v}. The disk keeps pushing and rolls the box a quarter
turn onto its +x face on the platform, {m_x, t}, with the disk still on the
face it pushed. Our planned route shares the pivot, then moves the disk round
the box's corner onto its top instead.

<video src="media/cmgmp/F1-lift-s0-00006_seed1.mp4" controls muted playsinline preload="metadata" width="100%"></video>

**CMGMP, lift instance 6, seed 1 (23 s, real time).** Passes under the
full rule. The box drops off the pivot once for 0.15 s and regains it before
the roll.

<video src="media/cmgmp/F1-lift-s0-00021_seed3.mp4" controls muted playsinline preload="metadata" width="100%"></video>

**CMGMP, lift instance 21, seed 3 (15 s).** Passes. The disk leaves the box
for a moment after the roll.

<video src="media/cmgmp/F1-lift-s0-00018_seed63.mp4" controls muted playsinline preload="metadata" width="100%"></video>

**CMGMP, lift instance 18, seed 63 (15 s).** Passes, on the 64th seed: the
same route, found late.

### The redesigned search: lift 37 of 40, lower 40 of 40 {#d23-results}

The redesigned search ran tonight on 40 random lifting and 40 random lowering
instances, on elliptic contacts, with everything as decided: the gate at the
controller's friction, the most robust disk placement (5 candidates), box
transport and release edits, a search ordered by the value estimate V₀
(η = 1 + h/g), **no learned ranker** (every admissible edit equally likely),
and no retries. A call budget caps the search: the number of times the local
solver Λ may be run.

| Task (40 instances) | budget | solved | 95% CI | Λ calls per solve, median (range) | wall time per solve, median |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| lower | 64 | **40** | 91–100% | 10 (6–13) | 396 s |
| lift | 192 | **37** | 80–97% | 88 (52–148) | 572 s |
| lift | 64 | 6 | 7–29% | 52 (52–64) | 390 s |

On every solve the per-run check of the call bound (the paper's Theorem C)
holds. The three unsolved lifts at budget 192 ran out of things to try (the
search tree was exhausted), not out of budget.

**How the search lifts.** Every one of the 37 solutions has the same core:

```text
{m_x, g, s} ⇒ {m_x, g_v, s_v}   pivot: the box tips onto its floor corner against the step corner
{m_x, s_v, g_v} → {t}            release: the box tips onto its +x face on the platform
{t} → {m_z, t}                   make: the disk goes to the box's −z face
{m_z, t} → box on its +z face    release: the box rolls once more and rests fully on the platform
```

Before the core, most solutions first push the box flush against the riser.
The search found a way that lets the box go twice; it did not find the
held route, the indirect lift, which is now the target (with releases off,
these solutions are no longer available to the search). CMGMP's lifts also roll the box onto its +x face;
ours adds a second roll. Transport was tried 27 times and is in no solution.

<video src="media/d23/lift_00002_solved.mp4" controls muted playsinline preload="metadata" width="100%"></video>

**Redesign, lift instance 2: SOLVED (52 calls in the search, 4 on the
solution; 19 s).** Pivot, release onto the platform, make on −z, release. The
replay reproduces all 4 logged calls exactly (0.0 mm).

<video src="media/d23/lift_00016_solved.mp4" controls muted playsinline preload="metadata" width="100%"></video>

**Redesign, lift instance 16: SOLVED (88 calls, 7 on the solution; 31 s).**
The disk first pushes the box to the riser (make, release, make), then the
same four-edit core.

**Why budget 64 lifts only 6.** The run at 64 calls makes exactly the same
calls as the run at 192, just cut off: 33 of its 34 unsolved instances had
already reached {t}, one make and one release from the finish. Without a
learned ranker every edit is equally likely, so a node's priority falls by a
factor of about 7 per level, and the value estimate shifts it by at most
about 2.5. The search therefore tries every shallower branch before the
platform node, four edits deep. That is a ranking problem, which is what the
learned ranker is for.

**How the search lowers.** Every solution is one release off the platform,
half of them after making the disk's contact on the box's +x face. No
transports. The release still throws the box (known issue, below).

### Paired with CMGMP {#paired}

The same 25 test starts per task for both planners, the same goal test (the
box at rest; for the lift, fully on the platform), one CPU core each, wall
clock. A start counts within a budget if it was solved within that time.
Exact McNemar test on the starts where the planners disagree.

| | 60 s | 300 s | 1,800 s (30 min) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **lift**, ours (budget 192) | 0 | 0 | **24** of 25 |
| **lift**, CMGMP | 1 | 5 | 15 of 25 |
| lift, McNemar p | 1.0 | 0.06 | **0.012** (ours only 10, CMGMP only 1) |
| **lower**, ours | 0 | 12 | **25** of 25 |
| **lower**, CMGMP | 14 | **21** | 24 of 25 |
| lower, McNemar p | < 0.001 | **0.004** | 1.0 |

Plainly: **CMGMP is faster at short budgets; ours solves more lifts at 30
minutes.** Our wall time includes loading compiled code on one pinned core
and is dominated by simulating each call (median 396 s per lowering, 572 s
per lift); neither planner was tuned for speed. One scene, 25 starts per
task.

### A first learned ranker

A value network V₁ and a ranker π were trained on tonight's lowering run and
the 64-call lifting run (the solutions relabeled in hindsight). On 11 held-out
instances V₁ predicts the remaining Λ calls with a mean error of 0.19 calls
(the graph's hop count: 0.63; V₀: 0.77), and π puts its top choice on the
solution's edit 97% of the time (uniform: 24%).

Used in the search (95% learned, 5% uniform, so no edit is ever ruled out), on
**3 lifting instances from a seed the training never saw**, at budget 64:
the learned ranker solves **3 of 3** (in 44, 53 and 43 calls), the uniform
ranker none. Three instances are a small sample; it shows the mechanism, not
a rate. V₁ itself does not yet order the search. *(Update, Nov 10: on 40
unseen instances, paired with uniform, 40 against 3; see [above](#nov10).)*

<video src="media/d23/lift_s1_00002_learned_ranker.mp4" controls muted playsinline preload="metadata" width="100%"></video>

**Learned ranker, unseen lift instance (seed 1, instance 2): SOLVED in 43
calls (26 s).** The uniform ranker does not solve it within 64. The replay
reproduces the log exactly.

### The redesign's first lowering solutions, with a known issue

In the redesign's smoke test (three instances, a check of the code, before
the full run above) the search solved both lowering instances in 13 calls each. Each
solution is two calls: make the disk's contact on the box's +x face, then a
**release**: the disk pushes the box off the platform and lets it fall to the
floor. Both replays reproduce the logged calls exactly.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Known issue: the release throws the box

The release's push does not set the box down; it throws it. In instance 14
the box leaves at 1.46 m/s and lands 0.54 m past the predicted landing; in
instance 3, 0.19 m past. Both still end at rest inside the goal, so both
count. Releases also end in the same pose whatever formation they were asked
for. This was a property of the release's scripted push. Releases are now
off, and the release path as built is superseded by the principled-release
proposal (R1–R3).
:::

<video src="media/d23/v_linear_F1-lower-s0-00014.mp4" controls muted playsinline preload="metadata" width="100%"></video>

**Redesign, lower instance 14 (2 calls, 12 s).** make, then the release.
Watch the throw: the box lands well past the step.

<video src="media/d23/v_linear_F1-lower-s0-00003.mp4" controls muted playsinline preload="metadata" width="100%"></video>

**Redesign, lower instance 3 (2 calls, 9 s).** The same two calls; the box
lands 0.19 m past the prediction.

### Tonight's work: the lift's pivot

On elliptic contacts the lift stalled at its first hard step, the pivot
{m_x, g, s} ⇒ {m_x, g_v, s_v} (box flat against the riser tipping onto its
floor corner). The cause was a friction mismatch. The gate assumed the
simulator's disk–box friction, 0.99, and placed the disk 45 mm below the
middle of the box's face. The controller only uses 0.35, and from there it
could not tip the box: 0.01° over 680 samples. On pyramidal cones the same
pivot had passed only because the disk slipped up the face.

Two fixes, both decided by Aykut tonight:

1. **The gate uses the controller's friction, 0.35**, at the disk. The
   hard break that follows the pivot stays legal. *(Superseded on Nov 11 by
   the friction band: the gate and the tracker use 0.3.)*
2. **The disk goes to the most robust placement.** The gate is re-checked
   exactly at 5 placements along the face,
   and the one with the largest margin wins. This is an interim rule: in the
   long run a learned pivot skill chooses its own placement (a first one is
   trained; compared below).

With both, lift instance 2's pivot passes into exactly {m_x, g_v, s_v}, with
the disk 44 mm *above* the face's middle, and the search went on to a release
onto the platform. A side finding: the exact gate passes at every disk height
on that face, but the controller succeeds only from about 10 mm below the
middle upward, so low on the face the gate is no test of what the controller
can do. Checking 5 placements costs about 5.6× the gate at a node where
the disk touches the box.

The full run [above](#d23-results) uses this fix: every lift solution
passes the pivot. On 353 held-out pivot states the quasi-static realizer with
the robust placement passes 348, a learned pivot skill 337, and the two
together all 353.

**Since then:** Aykut's quasi-static route test has run (releases off; see
[the night of November 9–10](#nov10)). V₁ and the ranker were retrained on
the full lift goal on Nov 10 (V₁'s error on lift-goal pairs 1.03 → 0.33 calls;
the ranker's top-1 on lift steps 0.93 → 0.98); V₁ enters the order behind a
flag. The paired rerun of these networks was dropped: they were trained on
solves that are mostly releases and falls, and are to be retrained on held
solves.

## Earlier runs on pyramidal contacts (superseded) {#pyramidal}

Before the redesign and before elliptic contacts (Nov 8–9: simulator disk
friction 0.99, the gate at the simulator's friction, MuJoCo's pyramidal cones,
under which held boxes creep), the teacher search solved the sub-goals almost
always (119 of 120), lifted only with two learned skills (Λ<sub>qs</sub> tips
the box onto the step corner, a learned break skill flips it onto its side
against the corner, a learned roll skill sets it down: 5 of 10, 7 of 10 with a
tie rule for the success test, since shelved), and lowered none (0 of 40: the
only edit off the platform, a knife-edge transfer onto the step corner,
failed in 52 of 52 calls). Its lift goal accepted a box straddling the step
edge. These runs are not continued.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Three clips from those runs"}
<video src="media/break_rl_vs_qs.mp4" controls muted playsinline preload="metadata" width="100%"></video>

**break(g_v) from one start (lift instance 2, call 9; 9 s).** Top: the
learned skill Λ_RL lifts the floor corner off and holds the box on the step
corner. Bottom: Λ_qs from the same state only tilts the box further on its
floor corner. On the 84 break(g_v) states that search reached, Λ_qs succeeded
